14830:
Solicitous means showing a deep, active, attentive kind of concern for someone's well-being, comfort, or happiness — the kind of concern that makes you go out of your way to make sure the other person is okay.

The keyword here is active. A solicitous person doesn't just feel concern quietly on the inside. They express it outwardly through careful attention and considerate action.

Think of a nurse who keeps checking on a patient — adjusting the pillow, asking about pain levels, making sure the room isn't too cold. Or a host at a dinner party who keeps asking if you need anything, refills your glass before it's empty, and ensures you feel completely at ease. That is solicitous behavior. It's care in motion.

The word has two closely related meanings. The first is by far the more common one.

Meaning 1 — Showing attentive, caring concern for someone:
This is the everyday use. Someone is solicitous when they are watchfully, earnestly concerned about another person's comfort, health, or happiness.

"She was solicitous about her elderly father's health, calling him every evening and arranging his doctor's appointments herself."

"The hotel staff were remarkably solicitous, anticipating the guests' needs before they even had to ask."

Meaning 2 — Being eager or anxious to do or achieve something:
This is a more formal use, and it means being keenly desirous or nervously eager to accomplish something.

"He was solicitous to make a good impression on his first day at work."

"The young diplomat was solicitous to avoid any diplomatic offense."

Notice that in Meaning 2, the concern isn't directed at a person's comfort, but at getting something right. The underlying feeling is the same — a kind of anxious, focused desire — but the object is different.

What separates solicitous from plain, ordinary caring is the quality of anxious eagerness wrapped inside it. A solicitous person isn't relaxed about the other person's welfare. There's a slight tension in it — a quiet, underlying need to make sure everything is right.

This is important. The word captures both the warmth of caring and the slight restlessness of worry. It's not just "I care about you." It's closer to "I care about you, and I want to make sure you're alright, and I'll keep checking until I'm sure."

By itself, solicitous is a positive or neutral word. It describes a genuinely admirable quality — thoughtful, warm attentiveness toward others.

However, context can push it in a more critical direction. When you see phrases like "overly solicitous" or "too solicitous," the writer is suggesting that someone's attentiveness has crossed a line into fussiness, hovering, or smothering concern. Imagine a waiter who interrupts your dinner conversation every two minutes to ask if everything is alright. Or a parent who is so worried about their adult child that they call three times a day. That kind of excessive attentiveness can be described as too solicitous.

So the word itself is complimentary, but it lives near the edge of a behavior that can tip into being overbearing.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are all in the same neighborhood, but they are not the same.

Concerned is more neutral and internal. You can be concerned without doing anything about it. Solicitous implies that the concern has translated into outward, attentive action.

Caring describes a general quality of character. It's broad and warm, but it doesn't carry the specific sense of active, watchful attentiveness that solicitous does.

Attentive focuses on the act of paying close attention. Solicitous adds an emotional layer on top — the underlying worry and desire for the other person's well-being that motivates that attention.

Considerate is about being thoughtful of others' feelings. Solicitous is stronger — it suggests a more urgent, watchful concern, not just politeness.

Think of it this way: a considerate person holds the door open for you. A solicitous person holds the door open, asks if you need help carrying your bags, makes sure you've eaten, and checks later that you got home safely.

Solicitous is a formal, somewhat elevated word. You are far more likely to meet it in literary fiction, careful journalism, formal essays, or polished speech than in casual everyday conversation. It lends writing a tone of refinement and precision.

In casual speech, someone might simply say "he was so caring" or "she kept fussing over us." In more formal or literary writing, the same idea would be captured with "he was solicitous" or "she was solicitous of their comfort."

Here are the most natural ways the word is used in a sentence:

  • Solicitous about something → "She was solicitous about his recovery."
  • Solicitous of someone's comfort/needs → "He was solicitous of his guests' every need."
  • Solicitous to do something → "They were solicitous to avoid any offense."

Knowing the related forms will help you recognize this word in the wild:

Solicitously (adverb) — describes how something is done with care and concern.

"He solicitously arranged the blanket around her shoulders."

Solicitude (noun) — the state or feeling of being solicitous; deep, attentive concern.

"She was touched by the solicitude her colleagues showed during her illness."
One Final Image to Lock It In

If you want one image to anchor this word in your memory forever:

Picture a devoted grandmother who, the moment you walk through her door, immediately wants to know — are you cold? Are you hungry? Did you sleep enough? Let her get you something to eat. Here, sit in this comfortable chair. She is not asking out of habit or politeness. She is genuinely, actively, almost anxiously focused on making sure you are perfectly comfortable and well. That grandmother, in that moment, is the very picture of solicitous.
14831:
Solicitude is a deep, careful concern for someone's well-being, comfort, or safety — one that is warm and caring on the inside, but tinged with worry or anxiety on the outside.

Think of it this way: when you care about someone, you feel good things toward them. But when you feel solicitude, that care becomes so strong and so focused that it starts to feel a little like worry. You are not just fond of them — you are actively thinking about them, watching over them, hoping they are okay, and quietly anxious that they might not be.

Solicitude sits at the intersection of three feelings:

Love/Care + Worry + Attentiveness = Solicitude

It is never cold or detached. It always comes from a place of genuine warmth. But it is also not carefree or relaxed — there is always a slight undercurrent of concern running through it. A person feeling solicitude is not simply wishing someone well and moving on. They are dwelling on that person's condition. They are paying close, careful, almost watchful attention.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

This is important, because "solicitude" is often confused with words that are close but not quite the same.

Care is broad and general. You can "care" about thousands of things casually. Solicitude is narrower, deeper, and more emotionally loaded.

Worry leans toward the anxious, fearful side, and can be selfish in nature (you worry because you feel uncomfortable). Solicitude, by contrast, is outward-facing — it is entirely about the other person and their welfare.

Concern is perhaps the closest word, but it is flatter and more neutral. Solicitude is warmer, more tender, and more personal than concern. Solicitude has a human touch that plain "concern" often lacks.

Empathy is about understanding another person's feelings. Solicitude goes further — it is not just understanding, but actively, almost restlessly, caring about what happens to them.

Solicitude can appear in a few different flavors depending on the context:

1. Tender solicitude — the gentle, loving watchfulness of a parent over a sick child, or a close friend checking in on someone going through a hard time. It is soft and quiet.

2. Anxious solicitude — when the concern becomes more intense and worried. A spouse waiting for a loved one to come home safe in a storm. A doctor anxiously monitoring a patient. The caring is real, but the anxiety is louder here.

3. Dutiful solicitude — concern shown as a matter of deep responsibility. A nurse attending to a patient with careful, dedicated attention. A leader who loses sleep over the welfare of those who depend on them.

4. Excessive solicitude — solicitude can also be used to describe concern that goes too far, to the point of smothering or hovering. In this shade, it carries a slight negative tone — implying that the person's concern, though well-meaning, is suffocating or unnecessary.

To make this concrete, here are sentences that show the word in action:

  • "She watched over her elderly mother with great solicitude, making sure she ate well and felt no pain."

(Here: tender, loving watchfulness.)

  • "His solicitude for his students' futures was evident in the hours he spent mentoring them after class."

(Here: deep, responsible concern that goes beyond the minimum.)

  • "The ambassador spoke with visible solicitude about the plight of the refugees, his voice low and serious."

(Here: genuine, heartfelt concern about others' suffering.)

  • "Her excessive solicitude over her teenage son was beginning to feel more like surveillance than love."

(Here: the negative shade — concern that has crossed a line.)

It is not pity. Pity looks down at someone. Solicitude stands beside them.

It is not obsession. Obsession is self-centered and possessive. Solicitude is genuinely about the other person's welfare.

It is not indifference dressed up as politeness. Solicitude is always sincere. You cannot truly feel solicitude without actually caring.

If you want to remember this word for life, anchor it to this image:

A person who cannot fully relax because they keep thinking about whether someone they love is alright.

That quiet, warm, watchful, slightly worried state of mind — that is solicitude.

Since this is the noun form, it helps to know the family:

Solicitous (adjective) — the describing word. "She was solicitous about his health." This means: showing or feeling solicitude.

Solicitously (adverb) — the manner of doing something. "He asked solicitously whether she had eaten."

Knowing these forms means you will recognize the word even when it appears in a different shape in your reading.

In one sentence: Solicitude is the warm, attentive, slightly anxious concern you feel for someone you genuinely care about — a deep wish for their well-being that keeps you watching over them, even when there is nothing more you can do.
14832:
Solidarity means a powerful sense of unity among a group of people — a feeling of "we are in this together" — along with the active support and loyalty that comes from that feeling.

When people are in solidarity with each other, they recognize that they share something important: a struggle, a cause, a condition, or a goal. And because of that shared bond, they stand up for one another, protect one another, and work together — even when it costs them something personally.

Think of it like this: if your entire class refuses to take an exam because one student was treated unfairly, the class is acting in solidarity. Nobody is personally harmed by the exam, but everyone stands together for the person who was wronged.

Solidarity has two sides to it — an inner side and an outer side.

The inner side is the feeling: a deep sense of connection, shared identity, and mutual loyalty. It's the feeling that what hurts you also hurts me, and what lifts you also lifts me — even if we are different people living different lives.

The outer side is the action: actually doing something to show that unity. Speaking up, sacrificing comfort, joining a protest, going on strike, donating, boycotting — any action taken specifically because you stand with others.

Both sides matter. Solidarity that stays only as a feeling but never becomes action is considered weak or even hollow. Real solidarity shows up in behavior.
Solidarity vs. Words That Sound Similar

This is where most learners get confused, so let's untangle it carefully.

Solidarity vs. Sympathy
Sympathy means you feel sorry for someone from a distance. You feel for them, but you remain separate. Solidarity means you stand with them. You don't just feel sorry — you actively take their side and commit yourself to their cause.

A wealthy person might sympathize with homeless people without being in solidarity with them. A housing rights activist who organizes campaigns, speaks out, and advocates for policy change is acting in solidarity — even if they've never been homeless themselves.

Solidarity vs. Charity
Charity flows from a position of "I have more, so I'll give some to you." It is generous, but it keeps a distance between the giver and the receiver. Solidarity is more equal — it's not about giving to someone, it's about standing beside them.

Solidarity vs. Agreement
You don't have to agree with every belief or decision a person makes in order to be in solidarity with them. You only need to recognize that their cause or struggle is just and deserving of support.

For example, you might disagree with some of a labor union's specific demands, but still stand in solidarity with workers fighting against dangerous working conditions.
Where You'll See the Word Used

1. Labor and worker movements
This is perhaps the most classic use. Workers who go on strike together, refuse to cross a picket line, or resist their employer as a united front are showing solidarity. The famous slogan "an injury to one is an injury to all" captures exactly what solidarity means in this context.

2. Social and political movements
Groups fighting for civil rights, gender equality, LGBTQ+ rights, or racial justice constantly use the language of solidarity. When one marginalized group publicly supports another, that is solidarity. When people who are not directly affected by an injustice still speak out and march, that is solidarity.

3. International relations
Countries or people across the world can express solidarity with those suffering under war, disaster, or oppression — by sending aid, applying political pressure, holding vigils, or loudly condemning the wrongdoing.

4. Community and personal life
Even in everyday life, solidarity exists. Neighbors who come together after a flood, friends who stand beside someone being bullied, or a community that rallies behind a grieving family — these are all acts of solidarity on a personal scale.

What makes solidarity more than just "teamwork" or "support" is its moral weight. Solidarity usually implies:

  • A recognition of shared humanity or shared struggle. You see yourself in others' pain or fight.
  • A willingness to sacrifice. True solidarity often requires giving something up — time, comfort, money, safety, or convenience — for the benefit of others.
  • Collective power. Solidarity is the understanding that people are stronger together than apart. It's the force that turns individuals into a movement.

This is why the word carries such emotional and political power. It's not a light word. When someone says "I stand in solidarity with you," they are making a serious declaration — not just of sympathy, but of loyalty and commitment.

• "The miners refused to return to work, standing in solidarity with their injured colleagues."
  • "People around the world lit candles in solidarity with the victims of the earthquake."
  • "Despite their differences, the two communities showed remarkable solidarity during the crisis."
  • "The statement called for solidarity among all nations to combat climate change."
  • "Her solidarity with the protesters meant she was willing to lose her job to speak out."

Solidarity is the deep, active unity among people who stand together — especially in times of struggle or injustice — supporting and protecting one another as if each person's wellbeing were everyone's shared responsibility.
14833:
To solidify something means to make it solid, firm, or stable — or for something to become solid, firm, or stable on its own.

That's the heart of the word. But it lives in two worlds: the physical world and the abstract world. Both are equally important and widely used.

In its literal, physical sense, solidify means to change from a liquid (or sometimes a gas) into a solid state. It refers to the process of something hardening or setting.

Examples:

  • Water solidifies into ice when the temperature drops below 0°C.
  • Leave the melted chocolate in the fridge, and it will solidify in an hour.
  • The volcano's lava solidified as it cooled, forming new rock.
  • The glue needs time to solidify before you can handle the broken piece.

Notice something important: solidify can work in two directions:

  • You can solidify something (you cause it to become solid): "The cold air solidified the wax." — Here, you are doing the action to something else. This is called transitive use.
  • Something can solidify on its own (it becomes solid by itself): "The wax solidified overnight." — Here, the thing itself undergoes the change. This is called intransitive use.

Both are correct and natural.

This is where the word becomes truly powerful and is perhaps used even more often in everyday life. In this sense, solidify means to make something stronger, more certain, more stable, or more permanent — or for something to become that way.

Think of it this way: just as a liquid becomes firm and stable when it solidifies, an idea, a relationship, a plan, or a position can also "solidify" — meaning it becomes firmer, more established, and harder to shake.

Examples:

  • Winning three tournaments in a row solidified her reputation as the best player in the country.

(Her reputation became firm and unquestionable.)

  • The two countries signed a treaty to solidify their alliance.

(The alliance was made stronger and more permanent.)

  • After months of uncertainty, our business plan finally solidified.

(The plan became clear, stable, and decided.)

  • That one conversation solidified my decision to quit the job.

(The decision became final and firm in my mind.)

  • Spending time together during the trip solidified their friendship.

(Their friendship grew stronger and more lasting.)
The Key Relationship Between the Two Meanings

The figurative meaning is directly inspired by the physical meaning. When something liquid becomes solid, it:

  • Stops flowing (it's no longer uncertain or changing)
  • Holds its shape (it becomes stable)
  • Becomes harder (it's difficult to break or undo)

All of these qualities are what we mean when we use solidify in the abstract sense. A plan that solidifies is no longer vague and shifting — it has taken a clear shape. A relationship that solidifies is no longer fragile — it has become strong and lasting. A reputation that solidifies is no longer questionable — it is firmly established.

In the figurative sense, here are the kinds of things that are commonly solidified:

  • A position or lead — "The team solidified their lead in the second half."
  • A reputation or status — "The award solidified her status as a legend."
  • A relationship or alliance — "The deal solidified the partnership between the two companies."
  • A plan or idea — "After our meeting, the concept began to solidify."
  • A decision — "Seeing the results solidified my decision."
  • Power or control — "The new law solidified the government's control over the industry."
  • Support or a base — "He worked hard to solidify his support among voters."
  • Gains or progress — "The team worked to solidify the gains they had made."

Here are all the forms you'll encounter:

FormExample
solidify (base)"These events will solidify trust."
solidifies (he/she/it)"Cold weather solidifies the oil."
solidified (past)"Their bond solidified over time."
solidifying (in progress)"The plan is solidifying."

When you use solidify in the abstract sense, it almost always carries a positive or at least neutral tone. It suggests that something uncertain, weak, or fluid has become stable and established — and that is generally seen as a good or desirable outcome.

However, context matters. "The dictator solidified his grip on power" uses the word accurately, but the situation itself is negative. The word is neutral — it simply describes the process of becoming firm or established, regardless of whether the outcome is good or bad.

Physical sense: harden, set, freeze, congeal, coagulate, crystallize

Figurative sense: strengthen, cement, reinforce, consolidate, establish, entrench, firm up, confirm

Among these, cement and consolidate are the closest synonyms in the figurative sense and are often interchangeable with solidify.

Physical sense: melt, liquefy, dissolve, soften, thaw

Figurative sense: weaken, undermine, erode, shake, loosen, destabilize

Solidify means to make something solid, firm, and stable — or to become that way. Literally, it's about matter changing state (liquid → solid). Figuratively, it's about something uncertain or fragile becoming strong, established, and lasting. It is almost always a sign that something previously shaky has found its firm footing.
14834:
To soliloquize means to speak your thoughts aloud to yourself — not to another person, but as a spoken expression of what is happening inside your own mind. It is essentially thinking out loud in full sentences, as if you were narrating your own inner world to no one in particular.

The key idea here is that the speaking is real, but the audience is absent (or ignored). You are not having a conversation. You are not expecting a reply. You are simply letting your inner thoughts pour out through your voice.

This word is most at home in the world of theatre and drama. When an actor on stage pauses the action of the play and speaks their character's private thoughts aloud — not to any other character, but as if they are alone with their mind — they are soliloquizing. The speech itself is called a soliloquy.

The most famous example in all of literature is from Shakespeare's Hamlet. When Hamlet stands alone and says "To be or not to be — that is the question," he is not talking to anyone on stage. He is wrestling, out loud, with the deepest questions of his life. That is a soliloquy. And the act of delivering it is soliloquizing.

Why is this technique used in theatre? Because the playwright needs to let the audience inside a character's head. Since a character cannot literally broadcast their thoughts, they speak them aloud instead. It is a dramatic device — a window into the soul.

You do not need a stage to soliloquize. In real life, to soliloquize simply means to talk to yourself in a sustained, reflective way — especially about something you are working through emotionally or mentally.

Imagine someone pacing the kitchen, saying things like: "Why did I say that? I should have just kept quiet. But then again, someone had to say it..." — that person is soliloquizing. They are not talking to the room. They are processing their own thoughts through spoken words.
What Makes It Different from Just "Talking to Yourself"

Talking to yourself can be as small as saying "Where did I put my keys?" aloud. That is casual and trivial.

Soliloquizing carries more weight. It implies something more sustained, more reflective, and often more emotionally charged. When you soliloquize, you are usually working through something real — a decision, a conflict, a regret, a feeling. It has the quality of a speech, even if the only listener is the air around you.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Monologue — A monologue is a long speech delivered by one person, but it is addressed to other people (an audience or other characters). A monologue is outward-facing. A soliloquy — and therefore soliloquizing — is inward-facing.

Musing — To muse is to think deeply, but it can happen entirely in silence. To soliloquize requires speaking aloud. The voice is essential.

Ruminating — Ruminating is turning something over and over in your mind, and it is usually internal. Soliloquizing is ruminating that has found a voice.

• To soliloquize — the verb. "He tends to soliloquize when he is anxious."
  • A soliloquy — the noun. The actual speech or instance of soliloquizing. "Her soliloquy lasted ten minutes."
  • A soliloquist — a rare noun for a person who soliloquizes.

• After everyone left the room, she began to soliloquize about whether she had made the right choice.
  • The old professor would often soliloquize at his desk, speaking his arguments aloud before writing them down.
  • In the third act, the villain soliloquizes, and for the first time, the audience understands his true motive.
  • He caught himself soliloquizing in the shower again — full sentences, complete arguments, addressed to no one.
To soliloquize is to give voice to your private thoughts — to speak them aloud, alone, as though your inner world has briefly stepped outside yourself and begun to talk.
14835:
A soliloquy is when a character in a play speaks their private, inner thoughts out loud — alone on stage, or as though no one else is there — so that the audience can hear what is going on inside their mind, even though the other characters in the play cannot.

Think of it as the playwright briefly "opening a window" into a character's head. The character isn't talking to anyone. They are thinking out loud. The audience gets to eavesdrop on the character's soul.

In real life, you cannot see what another person is secretly thinking. In a play, the same problem exists. A playwright cannot just pause the story and tell the audience, "By the way, this character is terrified and is planning to betray his best friend." That would be clumsy and unnatural.

The soliloquy solves this beautifully. The character steps forward, the rest of the world seems to disappear, and they speak their truest, most unfiltered thoughts aloud. No masks. No pretending. Just raw honesty — because no other character is listening.

For something to be called a soliloquy, a few conditions are usually true:

The character is alone, or might as well be. Other characters either leave the stage, or the soliloquy operates under the theatrical agreement that the speaking character is in their own private world for that moment.

The speech is not addressed to another character. The character is not talking to someone. They are talking with themselves, or simply thinking aloud.

The audience hears it; the other characters do not. This is the key dramatic bargain. The audience is granted a secret, privileged access to the character's inner world that no other character in the story shares.

It is longer than a passing comment. It has weight and depth. It usually explores something significant — a fear, a moral dilemma, a plan, a grief, a realisation.

A well-written soliloquy typically uncovers one or more of the following:

  • Hidden feelings the character cannot or will not express to others (love, jealousy, shame, hatred)
  • Internal conflict — the character wrestling with a difficult decision
  • Secret plans or intentions that other characters in the story don't know about yet
  • A character's true nature, which may be completely different from how they behave around others
  • Philosophical reflection — the character contemplating life, death, fate, or meaning

This is why soliloquies are so powerful. They strip everything away and show you the real person.

The most celebrated soliloquy in all of literature is from Shakespeare's play Hamlet. Standing alone on stage, the prince speaks the opening line:

"To be, or not to be — that is the question."

He then goes on to wrestle aloud with whether it is better to endure the suffering of life or to end one's life entirely. He is not saying this to anyone. No other character hears him. He is simply a man alone with the heaviest question a human being can face, thinking it through out loud. The audience watches his mind work in real time. That is a soliloquy at its finest.

Other famous examples from Shakespeare include:

  • Macbeth seeing a vision of a dagger before he commits murder, questioning whether it is real or a product of his guilt-ridden imagination.
  • Juliet speaking into the night air about Romeo, not knowing he is actually below her balcony listening.
  • Iago in Othello, revealing his schemes and his genuine hatred to the audience, while remaining charming and trustworthy to every other character in the play.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are easy to confuse, so it helps to see them side by side in plain terms:

Monologue — A long speech by one person. A monologue can be addressed to other people who are listening. It does not have to be private. A soliloquy is a specific type of monologue — one that is private, inward, and not addressed to any other character. So every soliloquy is a monologue, but not every monologue is a soliloquy.

Aside — A very brief comment a character makes directly to the audience while other characters on stage supposedly cannot hear it. Think of it as a quick, whispered remark. An aside is short. A soliloquy is long, developed, and deeply exploratory.

Dialogue — A back-and-forth conversation between two or more people. A soliloquy is the complete opposite — there is no back-and-forth, no other voice, no exchange.

Apostrophe (literary) — When a character dramatically addresses an absent person, a dead person, or even an abstract idea (like "O Death!" or "O Fortune!"). This can appear inside a soliloquy, but the two are not the same thing.

While "soliloquy" is primarily a word of theatre and literature, people do use it in everyday life to describe someone who talks to themselves at length. If someone is alone in a room, pacing back and forth, talking out loud and working through a problem — you could call that a soliloquy, and everyone would understand what you mean. The spirit of the word travels well: it always means one person, alone, giving voice to their inner world.

If you ever need to define it in a single sentence: A soliloquy is a speech in a play where a character, alone or as if alone, thinks out loud — letting the audience hear their private thoughts, while the other characters remain unaware.
14836:
Solipsism is a philosophical idea — specifically a theory about reality and knowledge — that says: only your own mind can be known to truly exist. Everything outside your mind — other people, the physical world, even your own body — might be nothing more than images, thoughts, or sensations happening inside your consciousness, with no guarantee of any independent reality behind them.

Put even more simply: solipsism is the position that you are the only thing that definitively exists, and the entire universe you seem to experience might just be a vast mental projection — a kind of dream that you are having.

Think about how you experience the world. You see colors, hear sounds, feel textures, taste food, sense pain. But here is the thing: all of these experiences happen inside your mind. Your brain receives signals and constructs the experience of a world for you. You never actually touch "reality" directly — you only ever experience your own perceptions of it.

So how do you know there is a real world out there producing those perceptions? How do you know other people are truly conscious beings who think and feel, rather than just very convincing figures inside your personal mental experience? How do you know the universe existed before you were born, or that it will continue after you are gone?

Solipsism takes these questions seriously and arrives at a startling answer: you don't know, and you can't know. The only thing you can be absolutely certain of is that your own mind exists — because your mind is the one doing all the experiencing, and you cannot step outside it to check what lies beyond.

There are a few ways solipsism can be held as a position, ranging from extreme to moderate.

The strongest and most radical form — often called metaphysical solipsism — says that only you exist, full stop. The external world and other people do not actually exist at all; they are entirely products of your own mind. You are essentially a lone consciousness, generating your entire experienced universe from within yourself.

A somewhat less extreme form — epistemological solipsism — does not necessarily claim that nothing else exists, but insists that you can never know or confirm whether anything outside your mind is real. Perhaps the world is real. Perhaps other people exist. But you have no reliable way of stepping outside your own experience to verify this. Your knowledge is forever trapped inside your own mind, with no exit.

The mildest form — sometimes called methodological solipsism — is less of a sincere belief and more of a technique used by philosophers. It means treating your own subjective experience as the only reliable starting point when examining what we can truly know, without necessarily claiming that nothing else exists. Philosophers sometimes use this as a kind of intellectual reset button — a way of asking, "Okay, stripping everything else away, what can I be truly certain of?"
Why Solipsism Is Almost Impossible to Disprove

This is one of the strangest and most unsettling things about solipsism: nobody has ever produced a completely airtight logical argument against it.

Think about it this way. If you tried to argue against solipsism, any evidence you point to — a book that says solipsism is false, a friend who tells you they are real, a scientific experiment — all of it enters your experience only through your own mind. A committed solipsist can always respond: "Yes, but that book, that friend, that experiment — those are all just part of my mental experience. They don't prove that anything exists outside my mind."

This is why philosophers describe solipsism as "irrefutable" — not because it is correct, but because it is structurally almost impossible to argue against using evidence. Every piece of evidence you produce is filtered through the very mind whose exclusive existence is being debated. You are trying to use the suspected dream to prove there is something outside the dream.

Even René Descartes — the famous philosopher who tried to methodically doubt everything until he reached something absolutely certain — concluded "I think, therefore I am," meaning the only thing he could prove with certainty was that he himself existed, because the very act of doubting proved a doubter was present. But he could not get much further than that without making additional leaps of faith or assumption.
Why Almost No One Actually Believes It

Despite being so difficult to disprove, solipsism is almost universally rejected — including by most philosophers — for a simple practical reason: it is deeply unlivable, and it clashes with everything about how we actually experience the world.

When you stub your toe, the pain is real and immediate. When someone you love dies, the grief is real. When you are hungry, the hunger is real. The world pushes back on us constantly, with a consistency and force that makes it feel overwhelming unlikely to be a projection of our own minds. Other people behave in ways we do not expect, know things we do not know, and surprise us — none of which you would really expect if they were merely creations of your own imagination.

Solipsism also collapses under a strange kind of internal defeat: if only you exist, then the very concept of "other people" becomes meaningless. So does the concept of "truth," since truth would then just be whatever your mind decides. Language itself becomes pointless, because language is built for communication between minds. Most people find these conclusions too absurd to live by, even if they cannot deliver a perfect logical knockout blow against solipsism.

Outside of philosophy, "solipsism" has taken on a looser, more everyday meaning. When someone calls another person "solipsistic," they usually mean that person is profoundly self-absorbed — someone who acts as though only their own experiences, feelings, and opinions are real or matter, and who seems incapable of considering the inner lives of others.

For example: someone who constantly redirects every conversation back to themselves, who seems unable to empathize, who treats the world as a mere backdrop to their own personal story — such a person might be described as solipsistic. It is a stronger and more precise word than "selfish," because it implies the person does not just prioritize themselves, but seems to barely register that other people have their own rich, equally valid inner worlds at all.
How It Relates to Other Ideas

Solipsism sits at the intersection of several major philosophical problems. It is closely tied to skepticism — the broader tradition of questioning what we can truly know about reality. It connects directly to the problem of other minds — the puzzle of how any of us can know that other people are conscious, rather than being very sophisticated biological machines that merely behave as if they are. And it overlaps with idealism — the philosophical view that reality is fundamentally mental in nature rather than physical — though idealism does not necessarily go as far as solipsism does, since many idealists still believe other minds exist.

Solipsism is the claim that your own mind is the only thing whose existence is certain, and that the entire external world — other people, objects, events, the universe itself — may be nothing more than mental experience, with no guaranteed independent reality behind it.

It is more of a philosophical challenge than a seriously held worldview. Its real power lies not in convincing people that they are alone in the universe, but in forcing a genuinely uncomfortable question: what can we actually know for certain, and how do we justify our confidence in an external world and in the reality of other minds? These questions have driven some of the deepest, most rigorous thinking in the entire history of philosophy — and they remain, even today, without a perfectly satisfying answer.

Most people reject solipsism not because they have decisively defeated it with logic, but because they find its conclusion — that you might be the only real thing in existence — too strange, too lonely, and too unworkable to take seriously as a way of living. The questions it raises, however, are ones that anyone thinking carefully about the nature of reality will eventually have to face.
14837:
When we describe someone or something as solipsistic, we mean they operate as if their own mind, perspective, and experience are the only things that are truly real — and that the inner lives, feelings, and realities of other people barely register, or don't fully compute.

A solipsistic person isn't just self-absorbed in the casual, everyday sense. It goes deeper than that. On some level, they can't — or don't — genuinely process that other people have inner worlds that are just as vivid, valid, and real as their own.

The word comes from a philosophical idea called solipsism, which asks a radical question: "How do I know that anything outside my own mind actually exists?" The strict philosophical answer is: you can't prove it. You can only be certain that your own mind exists — everything else (the world, other people, their feelings) could theoretically be a projection of your imagination.

Now, almost nobody literally believes this in daily life. But when we call someone solipsistic, we're saying they behave as if this were true — as if their own experience is the master copy of reality, and everything else is secondary.
What It Actually Looks Like in Real Life

Here are some concrete pictures to make this click:

Example 1 — The Solipsistic Friend
Imagine a friend who calls you only to talk about themselves. When you share something difficult you're going through, they nod for a second and then redirect the conversation back to their own life. This isn't cruelty — they just genuinely don't process your experience as something real and weighty. Your inner world doesn't fully land for them, because their own is the only one that feels completely real.

Example 2 — The Solipsistic Leader
A politician who dismisses all criticism, contrary evidence, or opposing views — not because they're lying or strategically spinning, but because they genuinely cannot conceive that another person's take on reality might be valid. Their perception of events is reality, in their mind.

Example 3 — The Solipsistic Writer
A writer who produces work so wrapped up in their own private references, feelings, and assumptions that it makes no effort to reach the reader. It reads like a diary written for no audience — because on some level, no audience truly existed in the writer's mind while writing it.

Example 4 — The Solipsistic Child
A young child who thinks everyone at a party is staring at them — not out of vanity, but because in their developing mind, they genuinely are the center of the universe. Young children are naturally solipsistic to a degree; growing up partly means outgrowing this.
The Most Important Distinction: Solipsistic vs. Narcissistic

These two words are very commonly confused. Understanding the difference sharpens your grasp of both.

A narcissist knows other people exist and have inner lives — but believes they are superior to those people and craves their admiration and attention. Their self-obsession is competitive and outward-facing.

A solipsistic person goes a level deeper. It's not about being better than others. It's that other people's inner lives don't feel fully real to them. The solipsistic person isn't competing for the spotlight — they just genuinely experience themselves as the protagonist, and everyone else as background.

A helpful analogy:

  • A narcissist walks into a room and thinks: "Everyone here must be watching me, because I'm extraordinary."
  • A solipsistic person walks into a room and thinks: "I am the main character of this story. Everyone else is a supporting role in my experience of life."

Selfishness is about wanting things for yourself, often at others' expense. You can be selfish and still fully acknowledge that other people have feelings that matter — you just choose to prioritize your own.

Being solipsistic is more foundational. It isn't really about wanting. It's about perceiving. A solipsistic person may not even intend to ignore others — they simply can't fully access the reality that others' inner experiences are as vivid and valid as their own.

Selfishness is a moral failing. Solipsism is more of a perceptual or cognitive one.

In real-world usage, "solipsistic" is almost never used to describe someone who literally believes they are the only conscious being alive. Instead, it describes people who function as if that were true, to varying degrees.

You might say someone is mildly solipsistic — meaning they simply have a hard time taking other people's perspectives seriously and always tend to center themselves in every situation.

Or you might say something is deeply solipsistic — like a memoir so self-referential that it assumes every reader has lived the exact same life as the author.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "His solipsistic worldview made it impossible for him to understand why his employees were frustrated — to him, their concerns simply didn't feel real."
  • "The novel was criticized for being solipsistic — its narrator treated every other character as though they existed only in relation to him."
  • "There's something solipsistic about the way she processes arguments — she can only ever see her own side as legitimate."
  • "Growing up means gradually becoming less solipsistic — learning to genuinely feel that other people's experiences matter as much as your own."
A Summary You Can Carry With You

Solipsistic = treating your own mind, experience, and perspective as the center and measure of reality, in a way that prevents you from fully recognizing or valuing the inner lives of others.

It's deeper than selfishness. It's more subtle than narcissism. It's a mode of being in which the world is experienced almost entirely through one lens — your own — and other people's realities never quite achieve the same weight and realness as your own does.
14838: Before diving into the specific meanings, it helps to know the soul of this word: solitaire always refers to something that is alone, singular, or meant for one. That single idea threads through every meaning below.
Meaning 1: A Card Game for One Player

This is the most common meaning of "solitaire" in everyday life, especially in America.

A solitaire is a card game you play entirely by yourself — no opponents, no partners, just you and a deck of cards. The goal is to arrange the cards in a specific order following the rules of the particular version you're playing. The most famous version is called Klondike, where you deal cards into columns and try to stack all 52 cards into four foundation piles, one per suit, in order from Ace to King.

There are dozens of variations — Spider, FreeCell, Pyramid, Golf — but they all share the same spirit: one person, one deck, one puzzle to solve.

In British English, this exact same game is called "Patience" — because, well, it requires a lot of it. If you hear a British person say "I was playing patience last night," they mean solitaire.

On computers: Microsoft famously included a digital solitaire game (Klondike) in Windows starting in 1990, which introduced millions of people to the game. Even today, "playing solitaire" often just means opening that app or a website version of it. The game became almost synonymous with what people did on a PC when they had nothing else to do.

Why it's called solitaire: Because you play solo — alone. There's no one else at the table.
Meaning 2: A Single Gemstone (Especially in Jewelry)

In jewelry, a solitaire is a single precious stone — almost always a diamond — set alone in a piece of jewelry, without any surrounding or additional stones.

The word can refer to two related things:

  • The stone itself: "She received a beautiful solitaire as a gift." Here, the solitaire is just the lone diamond.
  • The ring (or other piece of jewelry): "He proposed with a solitaire." Here, it means a ring that features one diamond as its centerpiece, with no other diamonds decorating the band or setting.

A solitaire engagement ring is probably the most iconic and classic style of engagement ring in the world — a simple band with a single diamond raised at the center, all attention drawn to that one stone.

The key quality of a solitaire in jewelry is its simplicity and focus. Because there is only one stone, that stone must be of high quality, since nothing else distracts the eye from it. This is why solitaire diamonds tend to be the most scrutinized for cut, clarity, color, and carat weight.

Example sentences:

  • "The jeweler showed her a round-cut solitaire, nearly two carats."
  • "A classic solitaire never goes out of fashion."

Again, the core idea holds: one stone, standing alone.
Meaning 3: A Peg Board Puzzle Game

This is an older and less commonly known meaning, but still very real.

A solitaire (also called peg solitaire or marble solitaire) is a puzzle game played on a wooden or plastic board shaped like a cross or a circle. The board has holes, and each hole starts with a peg (or marble) in it, except for one hole in the center, which is left empty.

How you play: You move pegs by jumping one peg over another into an empty hole directly on the other side — exactly like jumping in checkers. The peg you jumped over is then removed from the board. You keep doing this until no more moves are possible.

The goal: To remove as many pegs as possible. The perfect outcome — considered a win — is to end up with exactly one peg remaining, sitting in the center hole where the empty space originally was.

This game requires careful logical thinking because one wrong move early on can make it impossible to reach the ideal ending. It's a true one-player puzzle.

You'll find this game sold as a physical board (often beautifully made from wood) in gift shops and toy stores, often labeled simply "solitaire" or "peg solitaire."

This meaning is rare in everyday conversation but accurate and worth knowing.

A solitaire is the name given to two species of extinct, flightless birds:

  • The Rodrigues Solitaire — a large, flightless bird that once lived on Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean (near Mauritius). It was related to the famous dodo bird and went extinct in the 18th century, largely due to hunting by sailors and settlers.
  • There was also a bird referred to as the Réunion Solitaire, though there is some debate among scientists about how to classify it.

You will encounter this meaning mainly in books about natural history, extinct animals, or the history of the dodo. In casual conversation or modern usage, it almost never comes up.

The name fits: these birds lived and foraged largely alone, unlike many birds that flock together.
Meaning 5: A Type of Necklace (Less Common but Real)

In older usage and some formal contexts, a solitaire could also refer to a man's decorative necktie or cravat — a broad, loosely tied piece of fabric worn around the neck as a fashion item, particularly in 18th-century Europe.

Additionally, in some usage, a solitaire necklace is simply a necklace with a single pendant or stone — following the same logic as the jewelry meaning above.

These usages are mostly historical and rarely heard today, but they exist in older literature and fashion history.

——

Here's the simplest way to remember all the meanings:

Solitaire = something done alone, or something that stands alone.

  • A card game you play alone.
  • A gem that stands alone in its setting.
  • A board puzzle you solve alone.
  • A bird that lived largely alone.
  • A neck accessory worn as a single, solo piece.

The word you'll hear most in real life is in one of the first two contexts — either someone playing the card game (or its digital version), or someone buying or receiving a diamond solitaire ring. The peg board game is a distant third in modern usage.

If you see the word "solitaire" and need to decide which meaning is intended, the context will make it instantly obvious: a jewelry store ad, a card game, or a board with pegs are three entirely different worlds, and the word will fit naturally into only one of them.
14839:
Solitary means completely alone — with no one else present, no company, no companion. But it does more than the plain word "alone." It carries a sense of striking, total aloneness — one person, one thing, standing entirely apart from everything else.

Think of it this way: if "alone" is a plain, neutral fact, "solitary" is that same fact said with quiet emphasis. It makes you feel the aloneness, not just note it.

First: done alone, or experienced without others. When an action or experience is described as solitary, it means it happens with no other people involved. "She took a solitary walk at dawn" means she walked completely alone. "He spent a solitary evening by the fire" means the entire evening was his alone, with no company. The word often gives the sentence a calm, reflective mood — a solitary walk feels deliberate and peaceful in a way that simply saying "she walked alone" doesn't quite capture.

Second: a person who lives or prefers to be alone. When "solitary" describes a person's nature or lifestyle, it means they tend to avoid company, or their life is structured around being alone. "She was a solitary woman who rarely accepted invitations" tells you that by nature, she preferred her own company. "He led a solitary life in the hills" means his whole way of living was built around being alone. Importantly, this does not always mean the person is sad or suffering. Many people — writers, monks, scientists, naturalists — live solitary lives entirely by choice and find it deeply fulfilling. The word describes the fact of their aloneness, not a judgment about it.

Third: the only one — just one, with nothing else of its kind nearby. This is a slightly different but very important use. Here, "solitary" is close in meaning to "sole" or "single," but it goes further by making you visualize that single thing standing alone. "A solitary tree stood at the edge of the desert" — you can see it: one tree, nothing else around it for miles. "Not a solitary word was spoken" means not even one word — total silence. "She had not made a solitary friend in all her years there" means not even a single friend. In these sentences, the word is often used to emphasize how rare, scarce, or absent something is.
How It Differs from Similar Words

These four words are related but not the same:

Alone is simply factual and neutral — it tells you no one else is present. "I am alone right now." There is no emotional weight attached to it by default.

Lonely is emotional — it means you feel sad or pained because you are without company. You can be alone without feeling lonely, and you can feel lonely even in a crowd. "Lonely" is always about an inner feeling.

Isolated suggests being cut off from others, often by something outside your control — geography, illness, circumstance, or force. A village can be isolated by floods. A person can be isolated by illness or by others. There is usually a barrier involved.

Solitary is different from all three. It describes a real, physical state of being alone — and that state can be chosen or unchosen, peaceful or painful. Unlike "lonely," it does not automatically mean the person is unhappy. Unlike "isolated," it doesn't necessarily imply a barrier or external force keeping someone apart. A solitary figure can look dignified and serene, or bleak and tragic. The word opens the door — the rest of the sentence walks through it.

"Solitary" does not carry a fixed emotional color. Its tone shifts entirely depending on context.

It can be peaceful and positive: "She cherished her solitary mornings" suggests chosen, quiet time that she values deeply.

It can be purely observational and neutral: "A solitary lighthouse stood on the cliff" simply describes what is there — nothing sad, nothing celebratory.

It can be bleak or painful: "He died in a solitary room, forgotten by all" uses the word to underscore tragedy and neglect.

The word itself is emotionally open. Context does the work.

"Solitary" has a visual, almost cinematic quality. It doesn't just tell you something is alone — it shows it to you. "A solitary candle burned in the window" immediately places a single flame in the dark. "He was a solitary figure on the empty beach" makes you see one small person against a vast, quiet landscape. This is why the word appears so often in literature and poetry — it makes aloneness visible and felt, not just stated.

Solitary confinement is a form of imprisonment where a person is kept locked entirely alone, separated from all other inmates. It is considered severe punishment because human beings have a deep need for social contact, and prolonged isolation causes serious psychological harm.

Solitary animal is a term used in biology and nature. A solitary animal is one that lives, hunts, and survives on its own rather than in groups or packs. Tigers, bears, leopards, and orangutans are solitary animals. Wolves, lions, and meerkats, by contrast, are social animals. The distinction matters because it shapes the animal's entire behavior and survival strategy.

A solitary pursuit refers to any activity that a person does alone, requiring no others — reading, writing, painting, long-distance running, or fishing, for example.

A solitary example means the one and only example available — often used to emphasize just how rare or hard-to-find something is. "This is the solitary example of that painting that has survived" means there is no other.

Solitary, as an adjective, captures three related ideas: something done or experienced alone, a person who lives or prefers to be without company, and a single thing existing with nothing else of its kind around it. It is more vivid and emphatic than "alone," emotionally neutral unlike "lonely," and doesn't imply an external barrier the way "isolated" does. Its tone can range from peaceful to tragic depending on how it's used, which is precisely what gives it its quiet power.
